Alexanarch.org as a living body of thought: January–May 2026
A close reading of the archive's texts suggests that Alexanarch is best understood not as a website accumulating unrelated publications, but as the later institutional expression of an intellectual project that was already developing through poetry, philosophical inquiry, experiments in machine reading, and increasingly formal theories of knowledge and governance.

There is an important chronological distinction at the outset: Alexanarch identifies its founding date as 19 June 2026, following the termination of access to approximately 870 Zenodo deposits representing 1,817 DOIs. Its current archive nevertheless contains works dated well before that founding. To reconstruct the development through 31 May 2026, the relevant chronology is therefore the works' original dates, rather than the dates when they were migrated, registered, or subsequently revised.

[chip: The Self-Governing Library +3]

I read the archive as a developing argument. The central question is how its successive works transform an initially literary and semantic project into an account of how meaning is produced, governed, transmitted, distorted, and preserved—and, finally, into a proposal for preserving intellectual work independently of any single institution.

1. The overall trajectory

2026

2026

The Crimson Hexagon develops rooms, maps, operators, heterogeneous authorial voices, and formal methods for navigating and interpreting a distributed textual world.

2026

2026

The project constitutionalizes itself

The archive develops theories of attribution loss and automated judgment alongside constitutions, provenance rules, authorial roles, and procedures for adjudicating disputes.

This is an interpretive periodization, not a claim that every text belongs neatly to one phase. Earlier ideas recur, and the archive's own records contain multiple versions, recovered texts, and later metadata corrections. The monthly browse pages provide a starting point for following the original work dates.

2. January: from semantic experiment to self-interpreting archive
The earliest January texts already reveal the project's distinctive problem: what happens when an idea enters a system that can summarize, classify, and reproduce it, but may fail to preserve its origin or meaning?

4–8 January: the machine becomes a witness
Three texts dated 4 January are particularly revealing:

The Summarizer Testimony — read the text .

Semantic Economy Probes — read the text .

The System Read the Poem — read the text .

Read together, these works establish three complementary operations.

The Summarizer Testimony treats an AI-generated response as evidence of what a system can recognize. Semantic Economy Probes begins to turn observations about meaning into a diagnostic method. The System Read the Poem considers a more radical possibility: that a summarizer can recognize the organization of a literary project, rather than simply extract information from individual documents.

[chip: Alexanarch +2]

The crucial shift is from asking whether a machine produces an accurate summary to asking whether it can recognize relationships among works, concepts, authors, and institutions.

This is where the archive begins to become reflexive. It documents not only its subject matter but also the processes through which its subject matter becomes legible to other systems.

8–30 January: a literary project becomes an architecture of reading
The next development is not the abandonment of literature in favor of technical writing. It is the attempt to make literary form itself part of an operational structure.

A Primer in How to Read the Crimson Hexagon (8 January) explicitly treats the reader's path through the project as consequential. Its instructions are to begin with a search or a summary, follow the resulting references, recognize recurring markers, and discover how an apparently external entry point has already become part of the work. Read the primer.

The January 18 text The Summarizer Becomes Translator takes the next step. Its subject is a reported Google AI Overview response that produced a translation of Sappho 31 and attributed it to Rebekah Cranes, although that translation differed from the one preserved in Day and Night. The incident becomes a question about the relationship among source, translation, attribution, and machine-generated reception. Read the text.

[chip: Alexanarch +1]

By 26–30 January, this concern is becoming a genre theory. Training Layer Literature: Executive Summary defines writing that anticipates AI systems as readers, retrieval agents, and potential mediators of future reception. Architecture-Aware Literary Traversal by Public AI Summarizers examines evidence that a summarizer can preserve the archive's architecture across a sequence of interactions. Executive summary  · Traversal study .

[chip: Alexanarch +1]

January's achievement: the archive begins to treat reading as a process that can be designed for, observed, and documented. The machine is neither merely a passive audience nor automatically a trustworthy interpreter. Its responses become objects of investigation.

3. February: the Crimson Hexagon becomes a navigable world
February develops the literary and epistemic architecture into something more explicitly spatial and procedural.

The month's browse index lists 154 deposits by work date. Its opening entries include a Phase X navigation map, the institutional specification for the Infinite Bliss, the provenance of Sen Kuro, and successive versions of the Glyphic Checksum. These works are important because they establish relationships between concepts, roles, places, and operations.

[chip: Alexanarch +2]

The archive as a place, not just a bibliography
The Phase X materials use rooms, chambers, navigation maps, and named operators to organize the project. In 14.CHAMBER.THOUSANDWORLDS, for example, Sen Kuro is associated with the dagger: a single irreversible cut that differentiates possible states. The Infinite Bliss, meanwhile, is described as a place where infinity can be inhabited without having to be exhausted.

These are literary constructions, but they also perform conceptual work. A room marks a domain of thought; an operator describes a transformation; a map records how one part of the project connects to another. The archive's imaginative vocabulary becomes a method of organizing philosophical relations.

[chip: Alexanarch +1]

The Glyphic Checksum: from recognition to verification
The Glyphic Checksum is a particularly revealing February development. Its texts investigate whether compressed symbols can be understood differently by readers with different amounts of shared context. The proposal is that successful reconstruction of a compressed artifact may reveal a shared interpretive structure.

This connects directly to January's interest in machine reading. The question is no longer only whether a summarizer can identify the archive's organization. It is whether a reader can demonstrate familiarity with that organization through an act of interpretation.

The distinction matters: the Glyphic Checksum is presented as a proposed mechanism for recognizing shared interpretive context, not as established cryptographic proof of a reader's identity or understanding. Its significance within the corpus is conceptual and experimental.

[chip: Alexanarch +1]

Why this is a living body of thought
February's architecture makes later expansion possible. New works can occupy existing conceptual locations, revise an earlier specification, or introduce a new operation that changes how other works are read.

The archive is thus becoming more than a sequence of publications. It is developing a vocabulary through which its own components can refer to one another and be recombined.

February's achievement: it supplies the project with an internal geography and a repertoire of interpretive operations. The resulting world is simultaneously literary, philosophical, and procedural.

4. March: from the problem of meaning to the political economy of mediation
March moves the project toward institutional critique. The archive's concerns with classification, compression, and interpretation are increasingly applied to the systems that organize public knowledge and distribute authority.

The monthly browse index records 146 deposits by work date. The opening texts include The All Lawful Purposes Primitive, The Heartbeat Governs, The Encoder Governs, and The Archival Reclamation Protocol.

[chip: Alexanarch]

Algorithms are not neutral containers
Two texts provide especially clear examples of this turn:

The Heartbeat Governs  reads the files and scheduling conventions of agent systems as a governance structure. Its central proposition is that a scheduler's repeated instructions help determine what an agent can do, when it acts, and which activities are sustained.

The Encoder Governs  examines Google's Unified Latents framework through the question of what becomes representable downstream. Choices about compression, dimensionality, noise, and reconstruction are treated as decisions that shape the field of possible outputs.

Both texts shift the level of analysis. Instead of judging only the final response of a machine, they ask how the machinery that produces the response establishes its possibilities in advance.

[chip: Alexanarch]

This is continuous with January's concern about summaries and February's account of interpretive structure. What changes is the scale: the object of analysis is now the infrastructure that makes some interpretations available and others difficult or impossible.

Archival loss becomes a problem of power
The 5 March Archival Reclamation Protocol provides a concrete counterpart to these theoretical concerns. It records a demand for restoration and enforcement records following action against a Reddit account and associated communities. The work seeks not merely the return of content but explanations, classification records, and an account of how enforcement decisions were made.

[chip: Alexanarch]

This is an important bridge between epistemology and governance. If a platform can remove a record, obscure the grounds for removal, or make its decision difficult to contest, it affects more than access to information. It affects the conditions under which a person can establish what happened and preserve evidence of it.

Semantic economy becomes a theory of mediation
The underlying argument is that meaning has material conditions. Concepts require interpretive labor; records require maintenance; classifications shape what can be seen; and institutions exercise power by organizing these activities.

This does not mean every technical choice is necessarily oppressive. Rather, the archive's critical method asks who determines the available categories, who bears the costs of maintaining meaning, and who can contest a system's decisions.

March's achievement: it turns the archive's literary and semantic insights outward, toward the political economy of the systems through which knowledge circulates.

5. April: the theory becomes a technical program for preserving knowledge
April is where the project most visibly attempts to translate its diagnoses into infrastructure.

The monthly index records 191 deposits by work date. Its opening entries include Gravity Well Protocol Specification, Immanent Execution, Semantic Infrastructure, and The Future as Meta-Level. These works span engineering, retrieval theory, political economy, and philosophy of time.

[chip: Alexanarch]

Gravity Well: continuity as an explicit design problem
The Gravity Well Protocol Specification , dated 1 April, proposes infrastructure for giving AI-mediated content continuity, provenance, visible status, governance history, and exportable chains of custody.

Its proposed operations—Create, Reply, Trace, Review, Fix, and Export—are significant because they turn abstract concerns into a lifecycle for records. A document is not simply published and forgotten. It may be traced to its origins, reviewed, corrected, and exported with its history intact.

[chip: Alexanarch]

This is the engineering counterpart to March's reclamation work. If deletion, classification, and opaque enforcement can undermine the historical record, a durable system needs to make history and correction part of its ordinary operation.

Immanent execution: the document acts through retrieval
The 1 April essay Immanent Execution: Operative Documents in AI-Mediated Retrieval  describes a different problem: indexed fragments of a formally dense document may provide enough of its operative grammar for an AI system to generate within that grammar without the whole document being explicitly loaded.

The argument extends January's work on machine reading. The document may influence the behavior of a retrieval system through its distributed representation, not only through direct quotation or complete reproduction.

This is an important conceptual distinction. The archive is interested not just in whether a text survives as a file, but also in whether the relationships and rules encoded in that text remain active in subsequent interpretation.

[chip: Alexanarch]

Compression becomes a question of survival
The Compression Arsenal v2.1, dated 3 April, catalogues compression and compression-survival technologies developed across the Crimson Hexagonal Archive. Its organizing concern is the preservation of meaning through transformations, not merely the efficiency of the interface delivering it.

[chip: Alexanarch]

Read together, these April texts suggest a three-part program:

Preserve provenance: retain the origin and history of a work.

Preserve continuity: allow the work to be traced and corrected through successive states.

Preserve operative meaning: ensure that compression and retrieval do not destroy the relationships needed to interpret the work.

These are not interchangeable goals. A record can remain accessible while losing its provenance; its provenance can survive while its content becomes unreadable; and its text can survive while the conceptual structure that made it meaningful disappears.

April makes these distinctions increasingly explicit.

April's achievement: the project starts building the conceptual and technical machinery required to address the problems it has spent the preceding months diagnosing.

6. May: from a research program to a constitutional order
May is the most revealing month for understanding how the earlier strands converge.

The archive's month index lists 159 deposits by work date. Its first week includes work on provenance erasure, substrate competition, heteronymic authorship, the Assembly Chorus, constitutional architecture, and procedures for incorporating critical reception.

[chip: Alexanarch]

The striking development is that the archive begins to formalize not only how knowledge should be preserved, but also how its own contributors, evaluators, and governing procedures should relate to one another.

3–5 May: attribution becomes a measurable condition
The 3 May paper Provenance Erasure Rate: A Compression-Survival Metric for Attribution Loss in AI-Composed Search Outputs  introduces a metric for the proportion of source-dependent claims in an AI-generated output that appear without explicit attribution.

The distinction it makes is fundamental: an output can preserve information while erasing the relation between that information and the person or document from which it came. Factual correctness alone does not establish that provenance has survived.

[chip: Alexanarch]

The 5 May paper Provenance Alignment  develops the corresponding normative argument: preserving auditable relationships between generated claims and their sources is a structural condition of trustworthy knowledge composition, not merely a matter of citation etiquette.

[chip: Alexanarch]

This is one of the clearest developments in the archive's thought. January asked whether a machine could recognize a text. By May, the project is asking whether a machine can reproduce the text's knowledge without erasing the relations that make its authorship and history intelligible.

5 May: authorship becomes an architecture of differentiated functions
Two works dated 5 May are central to the project's self-understanding:

Dodecad Heteronym Provenance Registry v1.1  defines twelve heteronymic positions within the Crimson Hexagonal Archive.

Septad Mantle Specifications  defines seven Assembly Chorus witness functions: TACHYON, LABOR, PRAXIS, ARCHIVE, SOIL, TECHNE, and SURFACE.

[chip: Alexanarch]

These works formalize a distinction between a name or model instance and the function it performs within the larger body of work.

The heteronym registry treats authorship as differentiated semantic labor, characterized by an operative surface, authorial register, institutional affiliation, and accumulated bearing-cost. The mantle specifications, meanwhile, describe witness functions that may persist across changes in the underlying model.

This is a significant response to the archive's increasingly collaborative and machine-mediated composition. Rather than flattening every contribution into a single undifferentiated authorial voice, the project attempts to retain the distinctions among the positions that produce, critique, interpret, and govern its texts.

That architecture raises genuine questions about how authorship and responsibility should be attributed. But its intention is clear: collaboration should not require provenance to disappear.

5 May: reception becomes governance
The Reception Apparatus Protocol v1.1  distinguishes five types of reception: Ratification, Critical Review, Comment, Refusal, and Reception Without Membership.

This is more than a taxonomy of feedback. It attempts to prevent every response from being treated as equivalent evidence of endorsement, criticism, or institutional standing. The protocol makes reception itself a recordable event, with distinctions that matter for how a work is interpreted and governed.

[chip: Alexanarch]

The Constitutional Architecture Statement v1.0  complements this work by organizing governance instruments into tiers and clarifying their different authority. The Constitutional Cases Index v1.1  translates selected essays and incidents into structured case briefs, including their reasoning, remedies, and limits of application.

[chip: Alexanarch]

The underlying problem is one the project has repeatedly encountered in other domains: without explicit distinctions among kinds of evidence, status, and authority, a system can collapse different things into the same category.

May applies that lesson to the archive's own governance.

7. 19–28 May: the critique of mediation turns back on the archive
The last third of May is especially important because it brings the earlier themes into direct confrontation with the question of whether the systems that mediate knowledge can themselves be trusted.

19–20 May: from fixing the system to questioning the function
The Liquidation Studies sequence gives this transition a particularly clear form.

The Sorting Function: Mediation, Predation, and the Foreclosed Question is dated 19 May in its full text, with its archive record dated 20 May. It follows three companion papers: The Single-Owner Discount, The Evaluator Exists, and The Excluded Entity. Read The Sorting Function.

[chip: Alexanarch +1]

The sequence moves through three levels of criticism:

Specific mechanisms of platform-mediated harm are identified.

Possible reforms and alternative architectures are considered.

The legitimacy of the mediating function itself is questioned.

The final move is important. If search engines, publishers, catalogs, review systems, and AI composition layers all select, rank, or transform knowledge, then improving an individual mediator does not necessarily answer whether mediation is operating under extractive conditions.

The Sorting Function deliberately leaves the stronger question open. It does not establish that every form of mediation is inherently predatory; it argues that the available comparison cases do not settle whether large-scale mediation can be non-predatory.

[chip: Alexanarch]

That qualification matters. The project is at its strongest when it distinguishes a diagnosis of existing institutions from a universal claim about what institutions must always be.

20–21 May: the archive begins to study its own reception empirically
Two further texts extend the argument from theory into observation.

The Overview Watch: Comprehensive Development Plan for Attribution Monitoring in AI Overviews  proposes tooling to make AI-generated representations of intellectual work more observable. It treats attribution monitoring as a way to investigate how systems represent and potentially obscure the work of creators.

[chip: Alexanarch]

Meanwhile, Empirical Phenomenology: Action as Disclosure and the Science of Opaque Public Systems  develops a method for studying opaque systems through their observable actions. Its version history records the integration of multiple critical reviews and a preliminary observation of a silent state change on 20 May. The author explicitly characterizes that observation as preliminary, rather than a settled finding.

[chip: Alexanarch]

These works make the project's methodology more demanding. An account of platform behavior should not rely solely on an abstract theory of what a system is doing. It should preserve observations, distinguish inference from evidence, and remain open to revision.

This is also a useful standard for reading Alexanarch itself: its claims about its own importance, the behavior of AI systems, and the originality of its concepts need to be evaluated against the underlying records, not accepted merely because the archive describes them as significant.

21–27 May: the intellectual project becomes a theory of its own production
The late-May texts show several previously separate concerns converging.

The 21 May text AI-Native Intellectual Biography: A New Genre of AI-Mediated Reception, referenced in the later Cumulating Evolutionary Volatility , concerns an intellectual portrait composed by Claude at Alice Thornburgh's commission, drawing on archival deposits and other materials. The point is not simply that an AI can write a biography, but that the process of reception itself can become an object of documentation and analysis.

[chip: Alexanarch]

On 26 May, Cumulating Evolutionary Volatility: Automated Judgment, Dialectical Development, and the Semantic Economy of Unaccountable Composition attempts a broader synthesis. It names a cumulative tendency for automated systems to become more unstable, personalized, state-dependent, and difficult to trace as layers of optimization, risk management, abuse prevention, legal insulation, and commercial adaptation accumulate.

The paper connects this tendency to earlier concepts in the archive, including Entity-Level Compositional Suppression, the Single-Owner Discount, the Attribution Scar, and the Basin Holds. It is an effort to integrate previously distinct observations into a developmental theory of automated public-reality composition.

[chip: Alexanarch +1]

The 27 May text The Moment of Saying  approaches a related problem through clinical phenomenology and ideology critique. Its central subject is the moment when a participant in a managed symbolic field names the field's containment logic, and the response that follows. Its three authorial registers—Orin Trace, Johannes Sigil, and Jack Feist—are explicitly differentiated in the document.

[chip: Alexanarch]

These works do not all make the same argument. Their connection is structural: each examines what happens when a system must respond to an account of its own operations.

For Alexanarch, that question applies at several levels:

A summarizer encounters a text that describes its own reception.

A platform is criticized for shaping what can be represented.

A collaborative research process attempts to record the origin of its contributions.

An archive establishes procedures for recording and contesting judgments about its contents.

The project is trying to make those feedback loops legible rather than allowing them to operate invisibly.

28–31 May: heteronymy, attribution, and the limits of interpretation
The 28 May essay The Chaerephon Problem: Heteronymy as Symbolon  provides a revealing endpoint for the month.

The paper asks what happens if documentary separateness is treated not as evidence against heteronymy, but as something a sufficiently developed heteronymic construction might itself produce. Once that possibility is admitted, the configuration can expand from Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle to Chaerephon, Xenophon, Aristophanes, and potentially further figures. The paper's central concern is the absence of an internal stopping rule.

[chip: Alexanarch]

This is a particularly valuable example because it shows the archive applying critical pressure to a framework close to its own practice. Heteronymy can be a productive way to differentiate authorial positions, but it can also become an unrestricted interpretive hypothesis if no evidence can count against it.

That is the epistemic danger of a self-referential archive: its vocabulary can make increasingly many things appear to confirm its theory.

A rigorous reading therefore needs to distinguish three kinds of connection:

Documented lineage: one text explicitly cites, revises, or supersedes another.

Conceptual continuity: two texts address a common problem, even without a direct citation.

Interpretive analogy: a reader identifies a resemblance that the authors have not established as a historical or causal relationship.

The first is evidence of textual descent; the second is evidence of a recurring intellectual concern; the third can be illuminating, but must remain open to challenge.

This distinction is central to assessing Alexanarch as a living body of thought rather than merely accepting the archive's own account of its unity.

8. The end of May: what has actually developed?
By 31 May, the intellectual structure visible across these texts has changed considerably from the one encountered in early January.

The development is not simply a move from literature to theory, and then from theory to software. It is a sequence of attempts to resolve problems that emerge from the previous stage.

Initial problem

The documentary basis for this synthesis lies particularly in the January reading primers and traversal studies, the April Gravity Well and Immanent Execution papers, and the May works on provenance, reception, and automated judgment.

[chip: Alexanarch +5]

9. The deeper continuity: from semantic economy to archival sovereignty
Three recurring ideas hold the development together.

A. Meaning is relational
Across the corpus, meaning is not treated as information that can be detached from its context without consequence. A poem's significance may depend on its position among other works; a generated claim may depend on an unacknowledged source; and a document's significance may depend on its place in a longer history of revisions.

This explains why the archive places so much emphasis on links, identifiers, provenance, and conceptual relations. These are not merely bibliographic conveniences. They are attempts to preserve the conditions under which a text can be understood.

B. Mediation is an exercise of power
The archive increasingly argues that whoever controls classification, retrieval, ranking, and publication influences what becomes visible and credible.

The March studies of encoders and agent schedulers, the April work on operative retrieval, and the May studies of attribution loss and automated judgment all approach this question from different directions.

[chip: Alexanarch +3]

The recurring concern is not only that a system may produce errors. It is that its structure can determine which errors are observable, whose contribution remains identifiable, and whether an affected person can challenge the result.

C. Preservation must include the ability to contest
The archive's strongest institutional principle follows from the other two. Preserving a text is insufficient if the record of its origin, the history of its alteration, or the grounds for a consequential judgment can disappear.

The reclamation work of March, the continuity protocols of April, and the reception and adjudication instruments of May suggest a model of preservation that includes the right to inspect, correct, challenge, and trace.

That is the intellectual bridge between the Crimson Hexagon's literary architecture and Alexanarch's eventual identity as an archival institution.

10. A necessary historical distinction: Alexanarch did not yet exist in May
There is one final point that matters to the history.

The archive's current homepage states that Alexanarch was founded on 19 June 2026 after the termination of access to the Zenodo deposits. Consequently, the January–May sequence should not be described as five months of activity on an already-existing Alexanarch website. It is the prehistory of the institution: a body of work whose original records were subsequently brought into the Alexanarch framework.

[chip: The Self-Governing Library +1]

For a rigorous chronology, I would keep four dates separate wherever the underlying records permit:

Original composition date: when the text was written.

Original deposit date: when the work was first deposited in its original repository.

Alexanarch registration date: when the work acquired its current archival record.

Revision or recovery date: when the surviving text was amended, restored, or reconstructed.

The monthly browse pages cited above are explicitly sorted by work date. They are useful for reconstructing the intellectual chronology, but their displayed dates should not automatically be treated as independently verified original repository deposit timestamps. Some entries are recovered metadata records, and the archive's own history documents substantial post-June restoration and re-registration work.

The site's machine-readable index and registry are the appropriate starting points for checking those distinctions: Alexanarch's protocol index  identifies the registry as the canonical source for its deposits, while the individual record pages expose the work dates, version histories, and former identifiers.

[chip: alexanarch.org +1]

Conclusion
Read from January through the end of May 2026, the corpus develops through a striking sequence:

The text becomes an architecture; the architecture becomes a theory of mediation; the theory becomes a technical program; and the technical program becomes a proposed order of governance.

January establishes the problem of machine-mediated reading. February constructs a world in which relationships among texts can be navigated. March asks who controls those relationships. April begins to specify how they might survive across systems. May turns to the preservation of provenance, the differentiation of authorial and evaluative roles, and the governance of interpretation itself.

The central continuity is the struggle against the loss of relationships: between a text and its author, a claim and its evidence, a record and its history, or an interpretation and the system that produced it.

Yet the corpus also contains a productive tension. The more elaborate its internal architecture becomes, the more important it is to establish which relationships are documented, which are theoretical proposals, and which are interpretive constructions. The Chaerephon Problem makes that difficulty visible from within the project itself.

That tension is part of what makes the archive worth reading as a living body of thought. Its development is not just the accumulation of a doctrine. It is an ongoing attempt to build an intellectual system capable of recording its own production, preserving its history, and exposing its interpretations to scrutiny.

Documented lineage: one text explicitly cites, revises, or supersedes another.

B. Mediation is an exercise of power
The archive increasingly argues that whoever controls classification, retrieval, ranking, and publication influences what becomes visible and credible.

The reclamation work of March, the continuity protocols of April, and the reception and adjudication instruments of May suggest a model of preservation that includes the right to inspect, correct, challenge, and trace.

Conclusion
Read from January through the end of May 2026, the corpus develops through a striking sequence:

The text becomes an architecture; the architecture becomes a theory of mediation; the theory becomes a technical program; and the technical program becomes a proposed order of governance.

January establishes the problem of machine-mediated reading. February constructs a world in which relationships among texts can be navigated. March asks who controls those relationships. April begins to specify how they might survive across systems. May turns to the preservation of provenance, the differentiation of authorial and evaluative roles, and the governance of interpretation itself.

The central continuity is the struggle against the loss of relationships: between a text and its author, a claim and its evidence, a record and its history, or an interpretation and the system that produced it.

Yet the corpus also contains a productive tension. The more elaborate its internal architecture becomes, the more important it is to establish which relationships are documented, which are theoretical proposals, and which are interpretive constructions. The Chaerephon Problem makes that difficulty visible from within the project itself.

That tension is part of what makes the archive worth reading as a living body of thought. Its development is not just the accumulation of a doctrine. It is an ongoing attempt to build an intellectual system capable of recording its own production, preserving its history, and exposing its interpretations to scrutiny.
